entries.title: Trump Weighs Firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece After Reports of Misconduct
entries.summary: A senior U.S. official tells the AP that Trump and Secretary of State Rubio are "extremely pissed off."
entries.content:
By Matthew Lee

President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.

A senior U.S. official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.

In a series of stories, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.

Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the U.S. Embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.

After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”

But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations, saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.

“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.

The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.

A second U.S official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.

The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.

The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.

The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.

Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.

While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.

Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.

Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr.

entries.title: Capitals Fall to Kraken, 5-3, Despite Ovechkin's First Goal
entries.summary: The veteran forward scored his first goal of his 22nd season and No. 930 in his career.
entries.content:
Jared McCann broke a tie with 5:27 left and the Seattle Kraken overcame NHL career leader Alex Ovechkin's first goal of the season to beat the Washington Capitals 5-3 on Sunday night.

Jordan Eberle, Frederick Gaudreau, Kaapo Kakko and Ryan Winterton also scored to help the Kraken improve to 4-2-0. Joey Daccord stopped 33 shots.

On the deciding goal, McCann cut to the middle and beat goalie Logan Thompson on a quick shot. Ryan Winterton iced it with 2:40 left.

Jordan Kyrou and Boone Jenner also scored for Washington as the Capitals dropped to 3-2-0. Thompson made 22 saves.

After back-to-back penalty kills, Seattle got off to a quick start, with Kakko sneaking in a rebound just 6:06 minutes into the game.

The Capitals responded with two goals in a 5:06 span. First, Kyrou buried a cross-ice feed from Cole Hutson for his first with Washington. Then, after a strong forecheck and forced turnover from brothers Aliaksei and Ilya Protas, Ovechkin got the puck alone in front and sniped a quick shot past Daccord for his 930th NHL goal.

After Eberle tied it with 10 seconds left in the first, the Kraken pulled ahead 3-2 with 6:36 to go in the second when Gaudreau slid a backhander past Thompson. The Capitals tied it 46 seconds into the third, with Jenner scoring off this own rebound.

entries.title: What, Exactly, Happened at the End of the Commanders’ Disastrous Tie?
entries.summary: Neither Dan Quinn nor Jayden Daniels could provide a satisfactory explanation after an ugly ending.
entries.content:
As soon as the clock hit zero, Dan Quinn ripped the headset off his backwards-ballcapped head and spiked it to the turf, in much the same way a well-prepared quarterback of a well-coached team might be expected to do with the football, when his team is out of timeouts and well within range of a game-winning field goal in the final, ticking seconds of a critical NFL game.

Whatever it was that happened at the inexplicable, chaotic end of the Washington Commanders’ 27-27 tie against the New York Giants, the one thing that didn’t happen is the one thing that was supposed to happen — quarterback Jayden Daniels spiking the ball, stopping the clock and setting up what would have been a 41-yard field goal for the overtime win.

And because that didn’t happen — and because, instead, Daniels tried to run another play, was tackled for no gain, then watched helplessly as the final seconds ticked off the clock — Quinn, the Commanders’ head coach, endured a lonely and halting journey from the field to the tunnel that leads to the Commanders’ locker room, as Northwest Stadium filled with a hazy mist cut with shocked disbelief.

He walked with a slight limp and his hands on his head, alone. At the 25-yard line, Quinn suddenly stopped and stood for a good, long while, hands on his hips, staring out at the spot where this Commanders season very well may have expired a few moments earlier.

“When the time [runs out],” Quinn would say, “it’s not a good feeling, knowing this moment is going to slip through our fingers.”

In the aftermath of the meltdown that cost the Commanders a desperately needed win against a division rival, there was much said about accountability and resilience, with a healthy dose of frustration mixed in. Daniels repeated some version of the same line — “We have to be better” — no fewer than six times. Terry McLaurin said bluntly: “That can’t happen.” Quinn said several times he was the one at fault.

“The right call is obviously to [spike] it and don’t put ourselves in that spot,” Quinn said. “That’s my responsibility, no one else’s…. It stings today, bad. You don’t get those moments back.”

What was missing was any satisfactory explanation for what, exactly, had gone wrong at the disastrous end of the game. Instead, the principals talked around it in generalities and platitudes, leaving gaping holes to be filled with conjecture.

“We’ve got to be better at situational football,” Daniels said. “It starts with everybody, from the top down. But ultimately it’s on me. We’ve just got to be better.”

Asked directly whether he was aware the Commanders were out of timeouts, and thus had no way to stop the clock from ticking down to 0:00, Daniels gave an answer that was open to interpretation.

“Yeah,” he said, in a way that made that word sound more like an interjection than an affirmative, “we’ve just got to communicate that. That’s the whole thing. It starts with me communicating to everybody in the huddle. And I think everybody would say that from the top down.”

When Quinn was asked directly whether Daniels knew the team was out of timeouts, he said, “I haven’t spoken to him. But like I said, this falls on me.”

As for those above Quinn in the organizational hierarchy — a group that includes general manager Adam Peters and majority owner Josh Harris — the only public statement came from Magic Johnson, a minority owner, who posted on X: “I’m in total disbelief my Commanders had such terrible clock management in today’s overtime game against the Giants. All we had to do was kick the field goal and we would have won the game!”

It is hard to overstate how important Sunday’s game was for the Commanders. A win would have left them at 2-3 and a game out of first place in the imminently winnable NFC East, with a game in hand against the first-place Giants in case of a tiebreaker. A loss would have sent them to San Francisco next Monday night at 1-4 — and 0-3 in the division — and may have all but ended the competitive portion of their season.

At 1-3-1, the Commanders are neither finished nor well-positioned for a playoff run. But the fact is, they have just three wins in their last 17 games, dating to October 2025. Quinn may not get fired over Sunday’s debacle (which also saw the Commanders blow a 14-point lead in the final eight minutes of regulation), but it is the kind of embarrassment that, historically, has gotten head coaches fired. At the very least, the next week is likely to be filled with rampant speculation to that effect. Quinn may want to avoid sports-talk radio for the next few days.

Endings such as the one the Commanders authored on Sunday can make it challenging for a coach to hold a locker room together. Asked how the Commanders can possibly move forward after Sunday, he said, “We will. They’ve been through a lot already in five games. The locker room — this is a tough team. … They are equipped to absolutely dig in and get rolling.”

Late Sunday afternoon, Quinn got an uncomfortable taste of the fan base’s disillusionment. After Peters, the GM, came upon Quinn standing in disbelief at the 25-yard line, still staring out at the field, they walked off the field together in silence. In Section 108, the fans in the seats just above the tunnel stood and booed. Some of them held their arms out wide, palms up: the universal gesture for, “What the hell was that?”

Quinn kept walking and eventually disappeared into the tunnel, never looking up.

entries.title: Democratic Candidates in Northern States Are Hammering Home Trump's Tariffs
entries.summary: The costly trade war has turned into a messaging opportunity for Democratic candidates — and has Republicans on the defensive.
entries.content:
Democrats are using the U.S.-Canada trade dispute as an opportunity to appeal to voters and industries that have direct economic ties to Canada in competitive districts.

The trade war has translated into higher costs that are front of mind for voters. And it has put Republicans on the defensive — at times they have even taken the rare step of breaking with President Donald Trump over his pursuit of the tariffs.

“If you want somebody that's going to fight to repair the relationship with Ontario and Quebec, my campaign is for you,” Democratic candidate Blake Gendebien, who is running in New York’s 21st Congressional District, which borders Canada, told The Washington Sun.

Gendebien is running against Republican Anthony Constantino for the open seat currently held by Republican Rep. Elise Stefanik, and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee moved Gendebien to its “red to blue” program last week. On Friday, a new poll by the Siena Research Institute found Gendebien ahead of Constantino by 4 percentage points in the district, within the margin of error.

The same day, the president visited upstate New York, where he appeared alongside the Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman and asked voters to support Republicans in a slate of House races, including Constantino’s.

In part because of the Trump administration’s tariffs, Democrats are seeing pickup opportunities in places that normally would be considered more of a long shot.

“New York 21 is a seat that Republicans shouldn't have to worry about, but there's a very real possibility that it will flip to the Democrats, and reason number one will be Trump's attacks on Canada,” Jim Kessler, the executive vice president for policy at Third Way, told The Sun.

In a statement to The Sun, Constantino defended the administration’s policies and position on Canada.

“President Trump is fighting to even the scales for the American people and make life better for everybody involved,” Constantino said. “I look forward to going to DC and helping bring the negotiations to a speedy conclusion.”

Gendebien and other Democratic candidates running in battleground states and districts are using positions like those to directly tie their Republican opponents to what they describe as unnecessary policies that are hurting voters already struggling with the price of groceries and fuel.

After trade negotiations collapsed late in the summer, the U.S. ramped up pressure on Canada. It announced 50% tariffs on certain Canadian goods worth billions of dollars in August, imposed a ban on Canadian imports of nearly $1 billion, and threatened a 50% auto tariff.

A Washington Post poll conducted in early September found that more than 60% of likely voters in Michigan oppose 50% tariffs on Canadian imports.

Republican Rep. Tom Barrett, who is in a competitive race for reelection in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, has distanced himself from the president on issues such as the war with Iran. But his campaign is downplaying the effect of the Canada trade dispute on his race.

“I've seen plenty of polling that people don't like this fight with Canada, including Republicans, the overwhelming majority of Republicans, but it doesn't seem to be revealing itself as an issue in polling, or just in our interactions with people,” Jason Cabel Roe, a senior campaign adviser for Barrett’s campaign, told The Sun.

But Barrett’s opponent, Democrat William Lawrence, has incorporated Canada, the auto industry and tariffs into his economic message to voters.

“[Rep. Barrett] does whatever the president says, and the president is unqualified to set our tariff policy, but Tom Barrett can't admit that,” Lawrence told The Sun. “He votes in lockstep with the president every single time it matters, and we're all paying the price.”

Christina Hines, the Democrat running in Michigan’s competitive 10th Congressional District, told The Sun in an interview that in this year’s Labor Day parade celebrations in the state, workers waved the Canadian flag and held signs in solidarity.

“It's having real implications for people at their kitchen tables. The price of everything is increasing because of these tariffs,” Hines told The Sun.

“Those 50% tariffs on autos could decimate our industry, and the Trump administration has already handicapped the auto industry as much as it possibly could,” she added.

Her opponent, Republican Michael Bouchard, did not respond to The Sun’s request for comment.

In a statement to The Sun, the White House defended the administration’s position on the tariffs, arguing that Canada rejected “the most generous trade deal of any of America’s trading partners.”

“President Trump pledged to put always American workers, farmers, and businesses first and he has delivered by leveling the playing field for Americans,” Taylor Rogers, a spokesperson for the White House, said in a statement.

The dispute has also been a major issue in Michigan’s Senate race, where Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate.

“You're hearing somebody who has cheerled — again — a Canadian tariff policy that we are paying $5,600 a year for,” El-Sayed said of Rogers at a debate last Thursday. “The reason he's flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy. It has nothing to do with your costs. It has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers."

Rogers' campaign, through a spokesperson last week, acknowledged that the campaign has heard some voter concerns on tariffs.

“Just because they say that we're a rubber stamp for Trump's [trade] war doesn't make it true,” Abby Ronson, a campaign operative for Rogers, told The Sun.

Last Wednesday in a political advertisement, Rogers walked back his previous position defending Trump’s tariffs as necessary “when countries cheat American workers.”

“Prices are too high and Canada is not our enemy. We need to end the tariff war — now,” Rogers said in the video.

“I would like to see the deal made,” Rogers reiterated when pressed on the issue at the debate.

In Maine, the dispute is one of the clearest examples of a Republican breaking from the White House.

“Senator Collins opposes the Canadian tariffs and she has voted against them repeatedly,” a spokesperson for Republican Sen. Susan Collins said in a statement.

Troy Jackson, the Democrat running to replace Collins, continues to tie the senator’s campaign to the administration’s policies.

“Troy spent most of his life working along the Canadian border, so he knows how important this relationship is to Maine’s economy, and he sees Trump’s tariffs for what they are: a tax on Maine families and small businesses,” Dan Gottlieb, a spokesperson for the Jackson campaign, told The Sun.

entries.title: Congress Didn’t Act. Then the Issues Appeared on the Ballot.
entries.summary: An analysis of propositions on the ballot nationwide found that issues Congress focused on are now appearing in measures at a more local level.
entries.content:
Voters in several states will get the chance to do what congressional Republicans tried and failed to do: approve a measure to require voter ID at the polls.

Ballot initiatives to require voter ID await voters in California, Nevada, Arizona, North Carolina and Ohio, as do scores of other issues that will be decided on Election Day. Voters in some states will weigh in on redistricting, tax measures, marijuana regulations and traffic cameras. In Idaho, a state question will ask voters to choose the state’s official firearm.

Across the country, state lawmakers have put on the ballot the issues federal lawmakers haven’t taken up from either side of the aisle, according to a Washington Sun analysis of over 100 state ballot questions across the country.

“There’s a central playbook where D.C. funnels down into the states these various initiatives and ballot measures to achieve policy goals that they can’t achieve on the federal level,” said Randy Keating, a Democratic City Council member in Tempe, Arizona, who is fighting against the states’ voter ID requirement measure.

California State Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a Republican working in support of his state’s voter ID ballot item, said the measures are popping up right now because of low public confidence in elections, not a coordinated push.

The reason for a ballot measure is political inaction, DeMaio said, pointing to polling figures that show strong support for stricter voter ID laws.

It’s a “70% issue, and yet our politicians can’t get their shit together to get it done,” DeMaio said of strengthening voter ID laws. “We have to go to a ballot measure because politicians have failed us on both sides of the aisle on this important issue.”

The same thing is happening across the country on other issues. In more than 10 states, voters will be presented propositions on how their states handle taxes. Colorado, Missouri and Maryland voters will be asked about redistricting. And voters in Colorado, Nebraska and Washington will confront constitutional amendments that, if approved, would ban transgender student athletes from playing on sports teams that align with their gender identity.

Logan Casey, the director of policy research at the nonprofit Movement Advancement Project, said that some ballot measures reflect a “tactical shift” in how to push policies otherwise unlikely to pass in those states’ legislatures.

Casey pointed to Colorado and Washington as examples. The two states, which largely vote for Democrats, have ballot measures targeting transgender students’ participation in sports — policies that have failed to pass through the states’ legislatures in prior years.

“Those are two states that have had sports bans and other anti-trans bills introduced many years in a row, but have never been successful advancing through the legislature,” Casey said. “So there, the motivation is ‘Well, maybe we can get these policies enacted if we take it to the ballot box directly.’”

In states where the measures are popular or already implemented, redundant ballot measures could be a way for proponents to turn out voters in a midterm year; midterms tend to have lower turnout rates.

“It’s a bit of a different tactic, where they presumably are wanting to keep this issue front of mind for voters because they perceive it to be a winning electoral strategy or a wedge issue for them to use to turn out their own voters in a consequential midterm year,” Casey said.

Keating, the Tempe council member, said he thinks Arizona’s ballot measure on voter ID is in part meant to motivate Republican voters.

“What we're seeing here is definitely a ploy to get the base of turnout for an unpopular president in, frankly, what is a terrible political environment for his party,” Keating said.

Similar ballot measures in different states are sometimes coordinated, said Mary-Beth Moylan, a law professor at the University of the Pacific who focuses on ballot measures. People see the measures as a way to get directly involved in a national political conversation, she said, but the measures require outsized spending and efforts.

“I do think people view the initiative process as a way to enter the national political discussion,” Moylan said. “I also think there are very organized big-money groups that cross state lines that are promoting particular ideas.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Football Players of Week 7
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts include a bell-cow back from Madison and a lockdown corner from Eastern.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

This past weekend of local high school football was marked by statement victories. From The St. James stunning a national power in Virginia to Seneca Valley breaking a decade-long drought against a crosstown rival, this week’s crop of All-DMV Players of the Week showed up in big moments. Here’s who stood out in Week 7:

Kash Carter, Junior, Quarterback, The St. James

The St. James earned a program-defining victory this weekend, knocking off national powerhouse St. Frances Academy, 28-20. St. Frances entered the matchup ranked second in the nation by MaxPreps and was in the midst of a 13-game winning streak spanning two seasons.

Carter threw for three touchdowns in the win, an impressive encore to his five-touchdown showing against IMG Academy last week. Carter’s efficient play has helped catalyze The St. James’ ascendance, a rapid rise that has brought national buzz to the D.C. area.

Zeke Hubbard, Senior, Defensive Back, Eastern

Before Friday’s matchup against rival Theodore Roosevelt, Hubbard scribbled the letters “POTY” on a black strip of tape that he stuck to his face. The acronym, short for “Player of the Year,” was intended as a message to the rest of the D.C. Interscholastic Athletic Association.

“These are the games I’m built for,” Hubbard told Eastern coach Roman Morris before the game.

Hubbard backed up that statement with a sterling defensive performance as the Ramblers earned a comeback 20-12 win over the Roughriders. The senior didn’t allow a catch to Roosevelt’s top target and was the driving force behind a second half comeback that gave Eastern its fourth straight victory and third in league play.

Khamarion Imes, Senior, Athlete, Seneca Valley

For the first time in over a decade, Seneca Valley won the “Battle of Germantown” against neighboring rival Northwest. Imes, who rotates between punter, kick returner, free safety, wide receiver and running back for the Eagles, accumulated more than 200 all-purpose yards and three rushing touchdowns in Friday’s 31-28 victory.

“He’s just a leader on the field with his play, he takes the slack off of a lot of the other players to play relaxed and play free,” Seneca Valley coach Quintin Cosby said. “Just a phenomenal ball player.”

Chace Irvin, Junior, Wide Receiver, DeMatha

Irvin produced two jaw-dropping plays in DeMatha’s 35-0 shutout win over Washington Catholic Athletic Conference rival Good Counsel on Friday. The first came in the opening quarter, when the junior reeled in a leaping one-handed touchdown snag from quarterback Tristan Sabb.

Later in the game, with DeMatha pinned deep in its own territory, Sabb found Irvin streaking across the middle. He took it 89 yards to the end zone as the Stags put a running clock on the Falcons.

Will Smoot, Senior, Running Back, Madison

Smoot made his season debut last week for Madison against Virginia Class 6 contender Westfield and quickly made his mark. The senior rushed for 167 yards and a touchdown on 20 carries as the Warhawks downed the Bulldogs, 20-6, for their fifth straight victory.

“Will is one of the really explosive guys that we have on our team,” Madison coach Justin Counts said. “We just know that if we execute and we make a hole for him, we’ve got an opportunity to score a touchdown every time he touches the ball.”

entries.title: Florida Law Is Pressuring Congressional Candidates on Stock Trades — And It’s Causing Major Confusion
entries.summary: Some candidates are facing questions about their responses to Florida’s new, vaguely-worded requirement for detailing their stock trading intentions if elected.
entries.content:
Earlier this year, Florida state lawmakers did something uncommon: They passed a law requiring all candidates for federal office to publicly declare whether they’d personally trade stocks if elected to Congress.

The Florida law addressed a growing concern, among liberal and conservative voters alike, that some elected federal officials are financially conflicted or, even worse, making public decisions that benefit their private stock portfolios. Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis signed the measure into law this April and personally championed it.

But the murky language in the new Florida statute appears to have spurred confusion among 2026 congressional candidates — with some even filling out their disclosure form incorrectly in a seemingly earnest effort to be fully transparent, a Washington Sun analysis of state records indicates.

Republican Ryan Elijah and Democrat Eliott Rodriguez both checked the box indicating they do plan to trade stocks if elected to Congress. But they told The Washington Sun they actually have no intention of trading individual stocks.

Elijah said he filled out the form in the interest of “full transparency” because he didn’t know how his retirement account, which holds stocks, would be managed. The Orlando-area Republican amended his federal personal financial disclosure in September after facing an ethics complaint for failing to itemize assets in his retirement accounts, according to Florida Politics.

“Full disclosure, I probably wish I would’ve just checked ‘no,’ but I still think it's the most honest answer to check ‘yes,’” Elijah told The Sun.

Elijah said his campaign had “zero guidance” on how to comply with Florida’s new stock trade disclosure law. And neither the law nor the questions on the declaration form address how candidates should respond if a family member will be the one making trades.

Elijah earned the support of Republican Reps. Anna Paulina Luna and Mike Haridopolos — vocal supporters of a measure to ban stock trading by members of Congress — in his successful primary bid to unseat embattled Republican Rep. Cory Mills. Elijah said they know he “was checking that box for transparency, and I'm fully with them on banning insider trading.”

Rodriguez, a Miami-area Democrat, also has no plans to trade individual stocks and is “fully committed to stopping the incessant and unpatriotic insider trading,” said his campaign spokesperson, Fernand Amandi. But like Elijah, Rodriguez checked the Florida disclosure box indicating he does plan to trade if elected.

Rodriguez has a financial adviser who makes financial trades on his behalf, and his advisers do not trade individual stocks as a “matter of practice,” Amandi told The Sun.

“Mr. Rodriguez has almost exclusively owned ETFs and mutual funds in his personal accounts but has traded very small amounts of individual stocks in the past,” Amandi said.

Florida’s push for transparency comes as restrictions on congressional stock trading remain wildly popular for Americans on both sides of the political aisle. But Congress has continued to reject bills banning or restricting the practice, including a measure the Senate killed in September — it had passed the House — when Democrats balked at a voter identification provision.

The confusing language in the new Florida law allows two congressional candidates who may have materially different stock trading plans to make the same declaration. Here’s how it’s supposed to work: A candidate can check the box indicating they don’t plan to trade as long as their investment activity is conducted through “a trust or similar mechanism which strictly limits his or her ability to influence or exercise control over decisions regarding the management of assets.”

That means they can check the “no” box even if they plan to trade or keep trading through specific arrangements. These could include pooled investments, such as mutual or private equity funds, in which they have no control over individual investment decisions. They could also include discretionary investment accounts that, in theory, give an adviser the authority to make trades without the client’s prior approval.

Of Florida’s 55 congressional nominees across both parties, three Republicans — Elijah and Reps. Randy Fine and Scott Franklin — and three Democrats — Rodrigez, L.J. Holloway and Rep. Lois Frankel — checked the box indicating they intend to trade stocks if elected to Congress.
Randy Fine AP-21139621329468 (3600x2400, AR: 1.50)Florida’s new stock disclosure law includes another requirement for congressional candidates: Anyone who has previously held federal office is also required to affirm whether they’ve traded stocks in the past.

Of the three sitting lawmakers who checked the box indicating they do plan to trade if elected, Fine reported that he had not previously made any trades while in federal office, while Franklin and Frankel reported that they had. Financial transparency is an area where Florida’s congressional delegation has historically struggled.

This decade, many have violated the disclosure provisions of the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act — a 2012 federal law that requires members of Congress to disclose certain transactions and cracks down on insider trading. Under the STOCK Act — unlike Florida’s law — even if an investment adviser or account manager made the trade on behalf of the member of Congress, it’s the lawmaker who’s responsible for filing a disclosure covering transactions over $1,000.

Both Franklin and Frankel have run afoul of the STOCK Act by filing late disclosures after the 45-day required reporting window.

Franklin “has used a professional investment adviser to manage his investments since before he was elected to Congress,” Melissa Kelly, a spokesperson for the Republican congressman told The Sun. She said he “only learns of transactions after they have occurred, when they are reported to him for purposes of complying with House financial disclosure requirements.”

Similarly, Frankel “does not personally trade individual stocks,” said a spokesperson for the Democratic congresswoman who declined to be identified by name in this story. “The bulk of her investments are held in mutual funds and ETFs where decisions regarding the purchase and sale of individual securities are made by professional fund managers, not by Rep. Frankel.”

Fine is the only sitting member of Congress who appears to have opened the door to trading stocks despite not having any previously reported activity while in Congress — though his financial disclosures show he holds a retirement portfolio containing individual stocks.

Both Fine and Holloway did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Other sitting members of Florida’s congressional delegation indicated they do not plan to trade stocks if elected this cycle but reported on their Florida form that they had previously done so, including Republican Reps. Brian Mast, Jimmy Patronis and Gus Bilirakis and Democratic Reps. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, Jared Moskowitz and Kathy Castor.
AP 25301575600177 (4077x2718, AR: 1.50)Wasserman Schultz told The Sun she does not personally trade stocks. A broker handles a “small retirement account” for her, she said.

“I’m not involved in the market decisions that the broker makes independently. It started at about $11,000 and isn't much larger now,” Wasserman Schultz said in a statement. “In prior years, I had to disclose any stocks or assets my kids held, which were also made independently.”

Castor did not share details about how she traded stocks in the past when asked by The Sun, but she noted that she “broke with my party to ban Congressional stock trading.”

“That legislation was the first step and we must go much further to root out corruption,” Castor said. “To me, public service is a public trust, and I would never violate the trust my neighbors place in me.”

Mast, Wasserman Schultz, Moskowitz, Castor and Bilirakis have each violated the STOCK Act by failing to disclose personal financial trades on time. Patronis does not appear to have ever filed a transaction report on any trades, so it’s unclear why he indicated that he had traded in federal office in the past.

“We have followed all previous rules and voted to support the Stop Insider Trading Act,” Patronis’ office told The Sun in a statement.

Some lawmakers reported on their Florida form that they had not previously traded stocks, but they have reported investment activity under the STOCK Act.

Republican Reps. Maria Elvira Salazar, John Rutherford, Greg Steube and Laurel Lee all indicated they do not plan to trade stocks and have not directly traded or controlled trades they reported in the past. Salazar, Rutherford, Steube and Lee have also filed late disclosures under the federal law.
Maria Salazar (5723x3815, AR: 1.50)Other candidates who currently serve in Congress — including Haridopolos, Luna, Republican Reps. Kat Cammack, Aaron Bean, Mario Diaz-Balart and Carlos Gimenez, and Democratic Reps. Darren Soto and Maxwell Frost — indicated on their Florida forms that they do not plan to trade stocks if elected and that they had not in the past. Luna and Diaz-Balart have filed reports under the STOCK ACT while in Congress.

Among other Florida congressional candidates who aren’t currently serving in Congress and haven’t been previously mentioned, 11 Republicans and 20 Democrats indicated that they do not plan to trade stocks if elected.

On the Senate side, Republican Sen. Ashley Moody indicated she does not plan to trade stocks in the future, but she disclosed that she had previously made trades. Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon also reported that she does not plan to trade stocks if elected.

As a member of the Senate, Moody has voted in favor of Republican-backed federal legislation — the Stop Insider Trading Act — that could have restricted stock trading for lawmakers. Nixon has called for an all-out ban with “no loopholes.”

Most federal and state laws governing stock trades for candidates have retroactive requirements for politicians to report their activity — not their plans to trade — but Florida’s law sought to get ahead of the curve. But not every candidate, especially first-time office seekers, has the means to get advice from an expert on how to fill out their form.

“Delegating discretion to a financial adviser is a common excuse, but does not strictly limit a candidate’s ability to influence decisions over stock trades as the form asks” — as clients can technically still fire or change their management relationship with the person working for them, said Tavan Pechet, an adviser with experience working with ultra-high-net-worth families and advises congressional offices from both parties on legislation to restrict members’ stock trading. 

“The form appropriately seeks to differentiate between a candidate having no legal ability to influence investment decisions, and a candidate merely promising not to call an adviser and profit when they can," Pechet said.

“The new Florida form may be well intentioned — and it’s hard for a short question to be precise — but for any candidate who might invest in the equity markets, it’s not always clear which box to check” Pechet said. “What you subjectively ‘intend’ to do may be hard to answer even if you want to be honest, and impossible to police if you just want to get elected.”

Pechet said that “adding two short words to the form could remove some uncertainty: ask about intent to trade ‘individual’ stocks in a manner other than through a ‘blind’ trust,” as the latter is specifically set up to limit one’s influence over their own assets.

“I might advise any candidates who intend to participate at all in the equity markets to err on the side of caution by answering yes regardless of their intended investments,” Pechet said. “And if candidates want to deny an intent to trade stocks, they could probably find a loophole to support that answer too. Either way, the new rule may not provide much useful information to voters.”
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Guarding D.C.’s Election
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 12, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: The Guard at the ballot box, water (!) in the reflecting pool and a Commanders game with no winner. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 6/10. A murky start but a winning finish, as clouds clear and sunshine returns. Highs near 70 are just right. Full forecast from Capital Weather.


THE LATEST

D.C. election officials have a simple message for the National Guard: Please don’t stand in front of our ballot drop boxes.

The plea from the city’s election board followed an uproar over footage circulating on social media that showed National Guard troops standing next to a ballot drop box in Foggy Bottom on Thursday, reports The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle.

Federal law generally prohibits soldiers from being deployed around polling places, and the National Guard was quick to apologize for what officials said was an innocent mistake.

“JTF-DC service members are directed not to monitor or secure polling locations,” said a Guard official in a statement, referencing the Joint Task Force that coordinates the deployment of 2,800 troops around D.C. at President Donald Trump’s order. “JTF-DC … remains fully committed to conducting its missions professionally, lawfully, and with respect for the public’s constitutional rights.”

The outrage over the incident in part reflects ongoing anxiety around the Guard’s deployment in D.C. Residents and officials have already asked the Guard to stop operating around schools, over fears that kids will be frightened or that families won’t even send them to class. On Nov. 5 a D.C. Council committee will hold a public hearing on residents’ experiences with the Guard.

There are also persistent concerns with the Trump administration’s threats to deploy federal agents around polling places ahead of the critical November midterm elections, and Trump’s repeated criticisms of mail voting — which is widely used in D.C.

Voting has started in D.C., with 55 ballot drop boxes now open across the city. A weeklong period of in-person early voting starts Oct. 26.





DEEP DIVE

Reflecting pool water (4032x3024, AR: 1.33)
Water began pouring into the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool this weekend, days after Trump said the attraction would be refilled. A National Park Service sign posted on the pool’s wraparound fencing notified pedestrians of the “final touches” being implemented, noting: “As part of the normal refilling process, the water may temporarily appear cloudy before clearing.”

Marcus, a German visitor and senior executive defense adviser who withheld his last name to speak candidly, said he was not impressed by the sights.

“Everything I see is fenced,” Marcus told The Sun’s Michelle Del Rey on Saturday. “This is fenced; the White House is fenced.”

“What’s wrong here?” he added. “It’s supposed to be a democracy where everybody can walk around.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

A senior D.C. official was killed in a scooter crash on Capitol Hill last Friday night, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports. Talib Shakir, who was 50, served as the director of the Mayor’s Office of Returning Citizen Affairs, helping formerly incarcerated residents reintegrate back into society. It was an experience he knew well: He served 25 years in federal prison on a homicide conviction, and was released in 2019. “Talib made the most of his second chance and dedicated himself to helping others do the same,” said Mayor Muriel Bowser’s office in a statement.

The National Park Service began removing hundreds of trees that “do not contribute to the historic landscape” from East Potomac Park on Saturday as part of the Trump administration’s renovation efforts, The Associated Press reports. A total of 169 trees were slated for removal Saturday, but more than 500 are being targeted, according to a Friday court filing.

D.C.'s educators are preparing to return to the bargaining table. The Washington Teachers’ Union held two community conversations last week in order to collect feedback ahead of a new contract campaign, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports. In a meeting for Wards 1 and 2, teachers and community members bemoaned the district’s testing heavy calendar. Educators in Ward 8 wanted to see alternatives for DCPS’s teacher evaluation system, IMPACT, which many believed was being “weaponized” against them. A draft report for the contract is expected in November. The current terms expire Sept. 30, 2028.

Capitol Hill Books sells books. That may sound obvious. Yet, about once a day, the store fields an angry call from someone looking to speak with their lawmaker, The Sun’s Ellie Silverman reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

Arch enemies: Arlington County is suing to stop the construction of Trump’s proposed Triumphal Arch, arguing the administration failed to complete a legally required environmental review process before barreling ahead with the development, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.





FROM MARYLAND

School’s out: Sidwell Friends’ lower school campus in Bethesda, valued at just over $8 million in January, is being offered for sale, The Washington Business Journal reports.





TRIVIA


What was the first presidential election D.C. residents were able to vote in?

  1. 1934
  2. 1964
  3. 1994
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

Dan Quinn AP - 26284754734903 (5963x3976, AR: 1.50)
Commanders 27, Giants 27: Well, that was a weird one. In a roller coaster game, Washington squandered a two-score lead and one final chance at victory when Jayden Daniels failed to stop the clock in the final seconds of overtime. The Commanders were well within field goal range but out of timeouts, meaning they could only watch as the clock hit zero on a frustrating divisional draw.

The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson breaks down all the action (and postgame reaction), while Dave Sheinin takes a closer look at the stunning final sequence that cost them a chance to win the game.

The Capitals split their games this weekend, beating the Rangers on Friday and then falling to the Kraken on Sunday. New additions Boone Jenner and Jordan Kyrou both scored their first goals for the team. They were joined on the score sheet for the first time this year by Alex Ovechkin, who got one right in front of the net on Sunday for Career Goal No. 930, for those counting at home. (The 9:30 Club sure was.)

The latest group of All-DMV football players of the week includes a bell-cow back from Madison and a lockdown corner from Eastern. See all of Noah Ferguson’s selections here.

What to Watch Today

NFL: Bills at Rams, 8:15 p.m. (ESPN)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.

entries.title: Morning Sun: Still Running With Trump
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Live from South Carolina. Mike Rounds scrubs the president’s name from his campaign website. A look at state ballot initiatives. Mike Johnson and Hakeem Jeffries on the trail. Democrats’ favorite northern neighbor. And: Florida’s confusing stock trading disclosure law. 

THE LATEST

In South Carolina, Republicans still believe in Donald Trump. At least one very prominent one, Sen. Darline Graham, does. At the one (and Graham says, only) debate of the general election fight with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews last night, Graham defended the Iran war and praised ICE — two areas where other Republicans under pressure are trying to put as much distance as they can between themselves and the president.

We were in Columbia for the debate last night. The race has drawn more attention with national Republicans almost ceding Georgia and North Carolina. Andrews is trying to be the next southern Democratic hero, and is pressing all the buttons other red-to-purple state Democrats are vigorously mashing right now. She is focused on prices: “cut taxes, cut costs, cut waste” read the campaign signs waved by her supporters ahead of the debate.

She’s also selling herself as an independent, and not the kind of Democrat from Blue America. She’s against Medicare for All, for example. On the debate stage, she took offense when Graham tried to tie her to socialism. After the debate, Andrews told reporters in the spin room she did not want any national Democrat to come to South Carolina and campaign for her.

Graham has no such qualms about her party’s national leader. After the debate, spokesperson T.W. Arrighi told The Washington Sun “I don’t think you’ll ever see” Graham looking for distance from Trump. Why? “South Carolina is still Trump Country,” he told us.

Other Republicans continue to think differently about Trump. In South Dakota, Sen. Mike Rounds appears to be the latest member of his party to scour references to Trump from his campaign’s website, The Sun’s Jenna Monnin reports.

In an archived version of his site, text underneath the “ROUNDS FOR SENATE” banner previously read, “Mike is endorsed by President Trump and is working for South Dakota every single day.” The line on the current homepage appears to have nixed the nod to the president. A large “ENDORSED BY PRESIDENT TRUMP” banner is now noticeably absent from the bottom of the site, and several references to Trump have been scrubbed from Rounds’ issues page.

Rounds’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment. But like Graham, he is feeling the heat amid a difficult moment for the incumbent party — recent polling shows independent candidate Brian Bengs potentially too close for Republicans’ comfort. The difference is, while Rounds is running away from Trump, Graham isn’t.

More: Federal Judge Orders Trump Administration to End Promotional Ads • Bill Gates Warns of ‘Grim Possibilities’ Without More Control Over AI • Trump Declares That Russia and Ukraine Have Agreed to an ‘Energy Ceasefire’

FROM THE STATES


If at first you don’t succeed: Congressional Republicans did not pass the SAVE Act but voters in some states will face a question at the ballot box about whether they want to require voter ID going forward. The Sun’s Manuela Silva dug into more than 100 state ballot initiatives across the country and found a voter ID question in California, Nevada, Arizona, North Carolina and Ohio.

It’s a “70% issue, and yet our politicians can’t get their shit together to get it done,” California State Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a Republican pushing the voter ID initiative, told Manuela. “We have to go to a ballot measure because politicians have failed us on both sides of the aisle on this important issue.”

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


Department of Faint Praise: The top two House leaders, Speaker Mike Johson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, are very active on the midterm trail this cycle despite public polling showing that voter anger toward Washington is near all-time highs, The Sun’s Paul Kane writes. Lucky for the leaders, they’re flying under the radar — or as Paul puts it, they simply lack the menace and notoriety in the public imagination to serve as political villains for ad makers in each party. Democrats want to talk about Trump, sparing Johnson from ads. Republicans want to talk about New Yorkers, but not Jeffries — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Mayor Zohran Mamdani make better villains.

Blame Hug Canada: How Democrats in northern states sound this month: “If you want somebody that's going to fight to repair the relationship with Ontario and Quebec, my campaign is for you,” Blake Gendebien, the party’s nominee in New York’s 21st Congressional District, told The Sun’s Raymond Fernández.

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


It's the first day on the job for Katie Zacharia, Trump’s new White House press secretary whom the president says “has been with me, in spirit, from the very beginning.” Get ready for Zacharia’s test drive in the briefing room Tuesday at 9:30 a.m.

More: Trump Weighs Firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece After Reports of Misconduct





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Florida tries and fails at political stock trade transparency: A new state law requiring all federal candidates to declare whether they plan to trade stocks while in office has confused many candidates and left many questions unanswered, The Sun’s Jenna Monnin reports. A candidate can check the box indicating they don’t plan to trade as long as their investment activity is conducted through trust or something similar.

That means a candidate can check no even if they do plan to continue trading through something like a mutual fund. Or, check yes out of concern that trades will be made in their name without their control.

That kinda defeats the purpose. Republican Ryan Elijah and Democrat Eliott Rodriguez, both candidates for Congress, checked the box saying they do plan to trade stocks in office — but both told Jenna they actually do not plan to. Elijah said his campaign had “zero guidance” on how to comply with Florida’s new stock trade disclosure law. He has a retirement account he doesn’t directly manage. Does that count? “Full disclosure, I probably wish I would’ve just checked ‘no,’ but I still think it’s the most honest answer to check ‘yes,’” he said.



More: Expect to See More Political Ads for Candidates You Can’t Vote For • Trump Administration Plans $65 Million Exhibit at Saudi Arabia’s ‘Expo 2030’ • Six Senators Call for Trump to Reverse Course on Russia Diesel Purchase





NOT US

  • America’s Elected Officials Are Living in Fear, by Nick Corasaniti for The New York Times
  • What Is John Fetterman Doing, by Sam Janesch for The Philadelphia Inquirer
  • How Trump aide Natalie Harp’s family broke apart — and polarized, by Terrence McCoy for The Washington Post
  • The Crew of Virtually Unknown Donors Powering the Rise of the New Left, by Maggie Severns, Anthony DeBarros and Kara Dapena for The Wall Street Journal




WEEK AHEAD

Trump holds a rally in Youngstown, Ohio.

Maine Senate debate between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson.

Georgia Senate debate between Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and Republican Rep. Mike Collins.Iowa's Senate debate between Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek.

Monthly Consumer Price Index released.

Alaska Senate debate between Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.

Maine 2nd Congressional District debate between Republican Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap.

FEC quarterly deadline.

Saturday

JD Vance participates in a CBS town hall in Michigan.

entries.title: Johnson and Jeffries Are Just Bland Enough to Hit the Campaign Trail
entries.summary: Voters may hate Congress, but today’s more anonymous leaders don’t draw the anger like Pelosi or Ryan did.
entries.content:
With voter anger toward Washington near all-time highs, congressional leaders might be expected to hide out until after Election Day to avoid giving their candidates any sense of establishment support.

Instead, some leaders are fanning out across the nation and appearing in public to try to boost candidates in the key races. House Speaker Mike Johnson trekked across the Northeast and Midwest last week to appear with Republicans in a handful of battlegrounds.

And over the weekend House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries jumped from North Jersey into the Philadelphia suburbs to boost a pair of challengers facing popular Republicans with longtime brands in their districts.

This fall is not playing out like the “Fire Pelosi” wave of 2010, when a sign with that motto hung outside the walls of the Republican National Committee for the final seven months before those midterm elections.

The House speaker at the time, Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-California), became the face of Republican campaigns and starred in what her advisers estimated to be $50 million worth of negative ads — similar to how Democrats in the mid- to late 1990s made then-Speaker Newt Gingrich of Georgia a recurring image in their campaigns against Republican candidates.

This era’s congressional leaders simply lack the menace and notoriety in the public imagination to serve as political villains for ad makers in each party.

For Democrats, President Donald Trump is the larger-than-life figure who animates their liberal base, not Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

“The Republican Party is so defined by Trump that Mike Johnson and John Thune have not become high-profile figures,” said Nathan Gonzales, editor and publisher of Inside Elections, an independent political analysis publication.

Despite almost four years as Democratic leader, Jeffries does not draw nearly as much attention from the conservative political media machine as do Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

“If Republicans are looking for a big-city liberal to demonize — even one from New York City — they have two higher-profile options in AOC and Mamdani,” Gonzales told The Washington Sun.

Polling on the favorability of these congressional leaders is not as plentiful as it is for presidents and those who have run for president, but it bears out the idea that they do not have large profiles among voters, particularly among the small percentage of independents who decide late in campaigns and tend to determine the outcomes of close races.

In early September, Marquette University’s polling outfit tested all four leaders, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who has been in the spotlight the longest and, not surprisingly, is the least popular of the so-called Big Four.

Only 20% of all adults have a favorable impression of Schumer, while 54% hold an unfavorable impression, with close to a third of Americans expressing very unfavorable views of the Democrat. His own party’s voters have soured on him: Just 32% of Democrats hold Schumer in a favorable light, while 44% view him unfavorably.

The other leaders have relatively better standings. Johnson draws strong favorability among Republicans, with a split of 49% to 17%, while 68% of Democrats view him unfavorably. Almost half of independents don’t know enough about him to hold a view of the speaker.

Almost 40% of all adults have no view of Jeffries, while 21% have a favorable image of the Democratic leader and 40% view him unfavorably.

Thune, who is not even two years into the post of majority leader, is the most unknown of the quartet, with 53% of adults saying they do not know enough about him to offer an opinion.

This anonymity, plus Trump’s omnipresence in politics, makes it easier for Johnson and Thune to parachute into battleground spots without turning it into a bad story for the candidates on the receiving end.

“Even though Democrats don't like Johnson and Thune, they don't really generate the same anger among base Democratic voters compared to Trump,” Gonzales said.

So, last week, Thune dropped into Minnesota to stump with former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya, the Republican nominee who is a long shot to win the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Tina Smith.

He said the quiet part out loud, about how his presence there was meant to signal to Republican donors that they should support Tafoya’s campaign. “Obviously, translating that into financial resources and support coming here is something we hope to see happen,” Thune told local reporters.

In Bucks County, just north of Philadelphia, Jeffries appeared alongside the popular Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, both of them trying to raise the profile of Bob Harvie, who is challenging Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

Despite the slight Democratic lean of Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District — Trump has narrowly lost it three straight times — Fitzpatrick has regularly won by large margins. With Shapiro cruising to reelection, Democrats hope Saturday’s event draws attention to Harvie’s underfunded campaign.

“A vote for the current congressman is a vote for the status quo. It's a vote for more of the same. But a vote for Bob Harvie is a vote for dramatic change,” told the crowd at a middle school in Yardley.

Johnson’s swing through four Pennsylvania battlegrounds included only a private stop with Fitzpatrick, who recently told The Sun that he doesn’t consider himself a member of the Republican Party anymore.

Otherwise, Johnson barnstormed across the state, drawing out local press to cover events that might otherwise get skipped if it was just Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan at a contracting services garage in Hazelton.

“He's got a big target on his back because he's very, very good at what he does,” Johnson said of Bresnahan to a local TV station.

The same day, he appeared in the Lehigh Valley touting Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, whose reelection bid is growing increasingly difficult.

"He's very, very effective at what he does, and he has a passion that is contagious," Johnson told local reporters.

Pelosi could not take this approach back in 2010, and in the ensuing years she was a sporadic presence at public events in swing districts. By mid-October 2010, only 29% of voters had a favorable view of the House speaker, and 56% had an unfavorable image of her, according to Gallup. Almost 60% of independent voters viewed her unfavorably.

The first woman to become speaker, she had a net favorable image her first term in the office, but then Republicans turned their political machine against her.

Democrats lost a net total of 63 seats in those midterms and remained in the minority until the 2018 elections, when then-Speaker Paul Ryan of Wisconsin took a mixed approach to stumping for candidates.

Ryan did a whirlwind tour of a dozen key districts in the final couple weeks of the campaign, but some events were closed-door to avoid drawing attention to the Republican candidate being tied to an unpopular congressional leader.

He left Congress at the end of 2018 with a net favorability rating of negative 16%, just three years after starting off with a positive rating of 13%, Gallup found.

Johnson, who is less well known than Ryan or Pelosi, has more freedom to move about these days than did those two former speakers.

Democrats did issue a statement denouncing the swing-district Republicans for campaigning with Johnson.

“The best way to shake up a broken Washington is for Pennsylvanians to vote these bums out,” said Eli Cousin, spokesman for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

But they have no plans to hang a “FIRE JOHNSON” sign outside their office.
entries.author: Paul Kane

entries.title: Judge Says the Government Lost ‘Its Credibility’ By Cutting Down East Potomac Trees
entries.summary: A federal judge said the Interior Department cannot cut down trees until at least Tuesday.
entries.content:
A federal judge ordered the Interior Department on Monday to temporarily stop cutting down trees at the East Potomac Golf Course and explain why it cut down hundreds of trees over the weekend.

Judge Ana C. Reyes said she was “thoroughly unamused” that officials gave notice at 4:55 p.m. Friday — minutes before courts closed for the holiday weekend — that the National Park Service would begin razing trees the next day.

“I do not know how I could have made it any plainer I did not want what happened to happen,” she said, adding that the incident had “cost the government all of its credibility” in the case.

The DC Preservation League filed an emergency motion Sunday for the judge to stop the tree removal, saying the Trump administration felled hundreds of trees, including healthy mature oaks and maples. The group is involved in a legal action against President Donald Trump's plan to build a new golf course at East Potomac.

The judge had earlier told the government that it needed to notify the court before taking irreversible action on renovation and construction.

The Trump administration told the group's lawyers over the weekend that the operation was proceeding faster than anticipated, and that 529 trees had been destroyed on Saturday and that hundreds of additional trees would be cut down imminently, the DC Preservation League filing states.

On Monday, lawyers for the government said approximately 430 trees have been cut down so far, and there are plans to cut around 299 more.

Kevin Griess, the superintendent of National Mall and Memorial Parks, told the court in a declaration filed Friday that the trees do not contribute to the historic landscape and were being removed as part of an older rehabilitation project.

"No healthy trees that are contributing to the historical golf course (such as healthy, historic cherry trees) will be removed as part of this project," Griess said.

But the preservation group said the "clear-cutting that is happening now," after Trump said that work on a new golf course would move quickly, "cannot be understood as anything other than a major, irretrievable further step toward implementation of the Washington National plan."

"These excuses can no longer be swallowed," the group's filing says.

This is a breaking news story and will be updated.
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian, Todd Ruger

entries.title: Federal Agents Reportedly Search Ilhan Omar's Home
entries.summary: The search was part of a criminal investigation, people familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
entries.content:
By Alanna Durkin Richer

Federal agents on Monday searched the home of Democratic U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, a frequent target of Trump administration criticism, as part of a criminal investigation, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The search was conducted by Homeland Security Investigations agents, said the people, who were not authorized to publicly discuss an ongoing investigation and spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity. More details about the investigation were not immediately clear, though Vice President JD Vance has in the past accused Omar of committing immigration fraud — an allegation she has denied — and has said he and a top White House official were trying to figure out how to investigate the Minnesota congresswoman.

An email seeking comment was sent Monday to a representative for Omar.

The Justice Department said in a statement Monday that HSI agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the department in the Washington, D.C., area but provided no other details. The street was blocked off Monday morning as HSI agents remained near the home.

“This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” the department said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, of which Homeland Security Investigations is part, referred questions about the search to the Justice Department.

Omar represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She was first elected to the House in 2018 and has been a member of what's called The Squad of female lawmakers known for their progressive views and pointed opposition to President Donald Trump, a Republican.

Republicans have raised questions about Omar's past since before she was even elected, including asserting that she had married her brother and committed immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies.”

“It certainly seems like something fishy is there, but everybody's entitled to equal justice under the laws,” Vance told reporters in May. “So we're going to investigate it. We're going to take a look at it. If we think there's a crime, we're going to prosecute that crime.”

In a separate interview with conservative podcaster Benny Johnson, Vance said without offering evidence that “we actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud against the United States of America.”

He said that he and deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had been discussing it and “trying to look at what the remedies are.”

“That’s the thing that we’re trying to figure out," he said. "What are the legal remedies now that we know that she’s committed immigration fraud. How do you go after her? How do you investigate her? How do you actually do the thing? How do you build the case necessary to get some, some, some justice for the American people?”

Omar’s office in March dismissed Vance’s claims as fabricated and defamatory.

“This is rich coming from someone who literally said they were willing to ‘create stories’ to redirect the media,” Omar’s chief of staff, Connor McNutt, said in a statement.

“This is a ridiculous lie and desperate attempt to distract from the pedophile protection party’s unpopular war of choice, increasing gas prices, and rapidly dropping polling numbers,” McNutt said of the vice president’s allegations and comments.


Associated Press writers Eric Tucker, Michelle L. Price and River Zhang in Washington, Kathy McCormack in Concord, N.H., Mike Catalini in Morrisville, Pa., and Meg Kinnard in Columbia, S.C., contributed.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Elon Musk Is the Biggest Known Donor in the Midterms
entries.summary: The trillionaire has given more than $276 million since July in support of Republicans.
entries.content:
By Jill Colvin

Elon Musk, the world's only trillionaire, has quietly become the biggest known donor in this year's midterm elections, doling out more than $276 million since July to try to save Republican majorities in Congress.

The numbers, first reported by the New York Times ahead of this week's federal filing deadline, were confirmed by Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for Musk's super PAC.

The money includes $158 million given to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates, one of the largest known political donations in American history, according to the Times.

Another $76 million went to America PAC, a Musk super PAC, which has once again built out a major turnout operation like the one it used to help elect President Donald Trump by knocking on doors in 2024.

Musk also provided $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, Ken Paxton. The race has been a major focus of Musk's efforts.

It's a dramatic turnaround since last May, when Musk said he intended to cut back on future political spending. “I think I’ve done enough," he said at the time.

Despite the cash infusion, Musk has generally kept a lower profile than in 2024, when he appeared on stage next to Trump at rallies, and in the early days of the president's second term, when he led the Department of Government Efficiency.

He had a falling out with Trump while leaving his government post, but the two have since reconciled. Trump presented Musk with the National Medal of Science last week.

Musk's net worth has fluctuated around the trillion-dollar line this year based on changes in stock prices, but he topped $1 trillion again last week according to Forbes magazine.

Republican have a gaping financial advantage over their Democratic counterparts — a disparity that has been a rare bright spot for a party that is bracing for major potential losses amid deep voter frustration over the president's performance, stubbornly high prices and the unpopular war with Iran.

They have been using the money to blanket the airwaves in the race's final stretch.

“These robust investments have allowed the G.O.P. apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history," Romeo told the Times.

Democrats responded to the news by accusing Republicans of using vast amounts of cash to mask their shortcomings.

“Republicans are hoping to buy these elections, injecting tens of millions into races to try and outrun their unpopular candidates, unpopular president, and unpopular economy,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Democrats' Senate Majority PAC.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Democrats Say the Search of Ilhan Omar’s Home Is a ‘Disturbing’ Abuse of Power
entries.summary: The congresswoman said she “will not be silenced.”
entries.content:
Rep. Ilhan Omar and other House Democrats accused the Trump administration of abusing its power by searching her home on Monday, just weeks before the midterm elections.

Homeland Security Investigations agents searched Omar’s home early Monday as part of a criminal investigation.

At noon, Omar posted on social media that she was “ok.”

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said.

“I will not be silenced,” she added.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Whip Katherine Clark and Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar called the search “deeply disturbing” and said it raised questions about the “continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries.”

“For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations. Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family,” the Democratic leaders said in a statement.

A search of this kind is highly unusual this close to an election, and multiple other Democrats came to Omar’s defense.

“It is no accident that this raid comes three weeks before an election where Rep. Omar is on the ballot,” New York Rep. Yvette Clarke posted. “This is part of the fascist playbook to rile up his supporters in advance of the midterms.”

Illinois Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García called the raid on Omar’s home “an extreme abuse of power and an escalation of a years-long campaign against her.”

“Trump should not be allowed to politicize the federal government against elected officials,” he wrote.

Trump has frequently criticized Omar, including spreading the idea that she had married her brother to conduct immigration fraud. No federal agency has produced evidence of those claims, and Omar, who was born in Somalia and immigrated to the U.S. as a child, has called them “disgusting lies.”

Her office has not responded to a request for comment on the search.

White House border czar Tom Homan said last month that Omar was subject to an “ongoing criminal investigation,” and he told Fox News on Monday that a search warrant had been executed in an investigation led by the Justice Department.

“There is an investigation, a warrant was served,” he said, adding that he “didn’t want to get ahead of Todd Blanche.”

Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Illinois) called the search an effort to “target and persecute” Omar.

“We must strip them of their weapons. We must dismantle DHS. I stand in solidarity with Omar and every member of our community persecuted by the Trump administration,” she wrote on social media.

Wisconsin Rep. Gwen Moore wrote that the Trump administration was continuing to “demolish democratic norms and abuse the power of the federal government” by searching Omar’s home.

In a direct-to-camera video posted on social media, Rep. Ro Khanna urged Americans to “stand up and speak out.”

“It is simply chilling that they are targeting political opponents in this way, and it is disturbing that they are targeting Muslim Americans and a Muslim American woman legislator,” the California Democrat said.

This article has been updated with additional comments.

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: Stumped
entries.content:
Good afternoon. Here’s what you need to know.

THE LATEST

Federal agents searched the D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar this morning as part of an unspecified criminal investigation, a highly unusual move this close to an election.

  • Omar and other Democrats accused the Trump administration of abusing its power.
  • “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar said. “I will not be silenced.”

THE ADMINISTRATION

Donald Trump is headed to Youngstown, Ohio, tonight to rally for GOP candidates. And he’s not the only one pitching in for Republicans in the crucial swing state: Crypto-affiliated super PAC Fairshake has dropped more than $2.5 million already this week in an attempt to take down Democratic Senate hopeful Sherrod Brown.

Happy Columbus Day: The White House celebrated the holiday by creating a new AI-filled website: “Sail On. Columbus Day is back.”

THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

Elon Musk is now the largest known donor in this year’s midterm elections, doling out more than $276 million over the past several months in an attempt to save Republicans from losing their majorities in Congress.

THE HILL

If that effort fails, Speaker Mike Johnson said over the weekend that he plans to remain his party’s House leader.

  • "If, heaven forbid, we lost the majority, I would expect my colleagues would call upon me to continue to lead the conference in divided government,” he told CBS’s Robert Costa.

THE COURTS

The Trump administration cut down hundreds of trees at the East Potomac Golf Course in D.C. over the weekend, enraging a federal judge on Monday and leading her to order the Interior Department to put down its saws. The judge had previously ordered officials to notify the court before performing any construction on the site.

  • “I do not know how I could have made it any plainer I did not want what happened to happen,” District Judge Judge Ana C. Reyes said, adding that the incident had “cost the government all of its credibility” in the case.
Another judge ordered the Trump administration to stop airing its controversial taxpayer-funded ad campaign, which critics have called “propaganda.”

  • But at least two of the ads aired after the court’s Sunday evening deadline, according to AdImpact data cited by The Washington Post. 

SPELL CHECK IS FREE
