entries.title: U.S. Archbishop Says Catholic Soldiers Should Not Serve on Hegseth’s Firing Squad
entries.summary: The archbishop who oversees the Catholic Church’s pastoral services to the military has condemned the proposed livestream execution of Nidal Hasan.
entries.content:
Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the Catholic Church’s pastoral services to Catholics in the U.S. military, is condemning the proposed livestream of the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan.

Broglio, in a statement Monday, also stipulated that any Catholic soldier assigned to the U.S. Army firing squad should ask to be excused from that duty, which he described as contrary to the teachings of the church. He joins other Catholic leaders in speaking out against the death penalty and the livestream plans.

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in 2009 at Fort Hood in Texas, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.

Broglio recalled that he presided over the funeral of Michael Grant Cahill, the only civilian killed in that attack.

The crime committed by Hasan "was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?" Broglio asked.

“The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio added. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheelchair to the whole world?"
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Trump Says He Had ‘Nothing to Do With’ the Raid on Ilhan Omar’s Home
entries.summary: The president has spread conspiracy theories about Omar’s marriage and immigration status for years.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump told reporters Monday afternoon he had nothing to do with the raid on the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar conducted by the Department of Homeland Security.

“I understand that they’re looking at her very carefully. I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me,” Trump said, calling Omar’s native Somalia a “non-country.”

“I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ, I have nothing to do with it,” he said.

The Justice Department said the early-morning raid on her D.C. home was executed by Homeland Security Investigations based on a warrant signed by a judge. The search relates to an ongoing criminal investigation, the agency said, without providing further details.

Within 60 days of an election, the Justice Department generally avoids taking action against political figures, although it is not forbidden from doing so.

Omar, a Democrat who is up for reelection in Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District, called the raid an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement.”

House Democrats accused the Trump administration of abusing its power, calling the search “deeply disturbing.”

Trump has long criticized Omar, spreading the claim popular in right-wing circles that she married her brother as part of an immigration scheme. No federal agency has produced evidence that supports that accusation, and Omar has denied it, calling the claims “disgusting lies.”

In January, the president said the Justice Department and Congress were investigating Omar’s finances, claiming she was worth more than $44 million.

Financial disclosures from earlier this year show the congresswoman reported less than $15,000 in a savings account, less than $15,000 in each of four retirement accounts, and between $15,001 and $50,000 in the Minnesota State Retirement System.
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian

entries.title: Republican-Aligned Super PAC Buys Ads in the Wrong Portland
entries.summary: Defending Main Street said a media vendor mistakenly placed about $25,000 worth of digital ads in Portland, Oregon, instead of Portland, Maine.
entries.content:
A super PAC that supports Republican candidates confirmed its media vendor mistakenly sent ads attacking Troy Jackson, a Democratic Senate candidate, to Portland, Oregon, instead of Portland, Maine.

A spokesperson for Defending Main Street said in a statement that its media vendor, the 1903 Group, mistakenly placed roughly $25,000 in digital advertising in the Portland, Oregon, media market over the past week — on the opposite side of the country from Maine, where Jackson is running to oust Republican Sen. Susan Collins.

“The error was identified, the ads were immediately stopped and corrected, and the vendor is refunding Defending Main Street the full amount of the misplaced spend. No donor funds will be lost as a result of the vendor’s error,” the spokesperson said.

The 1903 Group said the issue was “100% a Cross Screen Media error,” referring to a company within the group. The company said it stopped the incorrect campaign, got the ads into the correct Portland market and refunded the cost of the ads that aired in the wrong market.

The mix-up, first reported by The Intercept, attracted social media attention over the weekend from Oregonians, who were served an ad that focused on Jackson’s votes in Maine’s state Senate in favor of increases to sales, gas, property and income taxes, calling him “Taxin’ Troy Jackson.”

Dan Gottlieb, a spokesperson for the Jackson campaign, used the opportunity to hit Collins back.

“Susan Collins’ allies are so out of touch with Maine, they can’t even find it on a map. Good luck convincing Mainers you know what’s best for them when you don’t know which Portland they live in,” he said.
entries.author: Mara Hoplamazian

entries.title: Trump’s Taxpayer-Funded Ads Kept Running After a Court Ordered Him to Stop
entries.summary: The ads ran in over 400 slots after a Sunday evening deadline took effect, according to the groups that sued.
entries.content:
The Trump administration appears to have continued running campaign-style ads funded by taxpayer dollars after a federal judge ordered them to stop over the weekend.

The spots aired on “60 Minutes,” “ABC World News Tonight” and “America’s Funniest Home Videos" on Sunday night into Monday morning, The Washington Post first reported.

Groups that sued the Trump administration over the ads, including the advocacy organization Common Cause, told the court Monday afternoon that the ads ran in over 400 slots after 7 p.m. Sunday, when the judge’s order to cancel the ads took effect.

The White House told The Washington Sun that the Department of Homeland Security did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel the ads that ran Sunday evening, which was the final day the ads paid for by the government would run.

One of the ads, “Final Battle,” is very similar to one used during President Donald Trump’s 2024 campaign. It features black-and-white footage of Trump walking down a hallway and recordings of statements he has made about “communists, Marxists and fascists” and the “fake news media.” Court filings estimate the Trump administration spent more than $9 million on that ad alone.

Another, titled “Maduro,” features images of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in handcuffs, and statements from administration officials about the U.S. operation to capture him.

Common Cause and other groups told the court they were not asking to hold the Trump administration in contempt over the violation of the court’s deadline, but they did request a status conference to discuss next steps. The Trump administration is required to file a report on its compliance Monday evening.

The groups suing over the ads argue that the use of taxpayer dollars violates restrictions on government funds being used for propaganda.

In a hearing over the weekend, lawyers for the Trump administration did not deny that the advertisements were paid for by taxpayer funds that were originally appropriated for border security, technology and screening, though they did argue that the issue was moot and the court lacked the authority to hear the case.

Trump has characterized paying for ads with taxpayer dollars as “a rather standard thing to do,” and said on social media that he considers them to be “a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A.”

But going forward, he said, the ads will be paid for with money he raised for MAGA Inc., a super PAC founded in 2022.
